<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:compression}
Choose $r$ with $r\equiv-u\pmod \sigma$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compressed}
 \prod_{x=0}^{n-1}
 \frac{1+\zeta^{x-\pi(x)}}{1-\zeta^{x-\pi(x)}}
 =\Psi_{n,\sigma}(r)^\sigma,
\end{equation}
where, for a derangement,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Psi}
 \Psi_{n,\sigma}(r)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&N\text{ even},\\[4pt]
 \displaystyle i\cot\left(\frac{\pi r}{\sigma}\right),&N\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
As $x$ runs through $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$, the values
\[
 x-\pi(x)=(1-v)x-u
\]
run through the congruence class $r=-u\bmod \sigma$ in $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$, each value occurring
exactly $\sigma$ times.  Hence
\[
 \prod_{x=0}^{n-1}
 \frac{1+\zeta^{x-\pi(x)}}{1-\zeta^{x-\pi(x)}}
 =\left(\prod_{m=0}^{N-1}
 \frac{1+\zeta^{r+\sigma m}}{1-\zeta^{r+\sigma m}}\right)^\sigma.
\]

Since $\zeta^\sigma$ is a primitive $N$th root of unity (for $\mathrm{ord}(\zeta^{\sigma})=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,\sigma)}=\frac{n}{\sigma} = N$),
then
\[
 z^{N}-1 = \prod_{m=0}^{N-1}(z-\zeta^{m\sigma}),
\]
and, upon substitutions $z=\zeta^{u}$ and $z=-\zeta^{u}$, we have
\[
 (\zeta^{u})^{N}-1 = \prod_{m=0}^{N-1}(\zeta^{u}-\zeta^{m\sigma})=\prod_{m=0}^{N-1}\zeta^{u}(1-\zeta^{-u+m\sigma})=(\zeta^{u})^{N}\prod_{m=0}^{N-1}(1-\zeta^{r+m\sigma})
\]
and
\[
 (-\zeta^{u})^{N}-1 = \prod_{m=0}^{N-1}(-\zeta^{u}-\zeta^{m\sigma})=\prod_{m=0}^{N-1}(-\zeta^{u})(1+\zeta^{-u+m\sigma})=(-\zeta^{u})^{N}\prod_{m=0}^{N-1}(1+\zeta^{r+m\sigma}).
\]

Therefore
\[
(-1)^{N}\frac{1-(-\zeta^{u})^N}{1-(\zeta^{u})^N}=
 \prod_{m=0}^{N-1}
 \frac{1+\zeta^{r+\sigma m}}{1-\zeta^{r+\sigma m}}.
\]

If $N$ is even this ratio is $1$.  If $N$ is odd and
$\omega=\exp(2\pi i/\sigma)$, then $(\zeta^{u})^N=\omega^{u}$ and
\[
 -\frac{1+\omega^{u}}{1-\omega^{u}}
 =-i\cot\left(\frac{\pi u}{\sigma}\right)=-i\cot\left(\frac{\pi(-r)}{\sigma}\right)=i\cot\left(\frac{\pi r}{\sigma}\right).
\]

When $\pi$ is a derangement, $r\not\equiv0\pmod \sigma$, and thus no
denominator vanishes.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:translation-sign}
For even $n$,
\[
 \operatorname{sign}(e^u.1)=(-1)^u.
\]

Consequently, for $\sigma=\gcd(v-1,n)$ and $1\leq r\leq \sigma-1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residue-sign-sum}
 \sum_{\substack{0\le u<n\\u\equiv-r\, (\mathrm{mod}\,\sigma)}}(-1)^u
 =\frac{n}{\sigma}(-1)^r
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Translation by $u$ has $\gcd(u,n)$ cycles, each of length
$n/\gcd(u,n)$. Each one has sign $(-1)^{\frac{n}{\gcd(u,n)}-1}$ and therefore the sign
of $e^{u}.1$ is
\[
 ((-1)^{\frac{n}{\gcd(u,n)}-1})^{\gcd(u,n)}=(-1)^{n-\gcd(u,n)}.
\]

Since $n$ is even, and
$\gcd(u,n)$ and $u$ have the same parity, then
\[
 (-1)^{n-\gcd(u,n)}=(-1)^{n}(-1)^{\gcd(u,n)} = (-1)^u
\]

For the second assertion write $u=-r+j\sigma$, with
$1\leq j\leq n/\sigma$.  Since $\sigma$ is even then all signs are equal, and the total follows at once.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:refl} Let $n$ be even, $v\in(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times}$ and $\sigma=\gcd(v-1,n)$. Then the multiplication
permutation $e^{0}.v:x\mapsto vx$ of $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ has sign
\[
 \epsilon_{n}(\sigma)=(-1)^{\frac{\sigma\cdot(n/2-1)}{2}}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
When $n/2$ is odd then $\operatorname{sign}(e^{0}.v)$ is $1$ regardless of the value of $v$. When $n/2$ is
even, then it is $(-1)^{\frac{v-1}{2}}$. This is $-1$ if, and only if, $v\equiv 3\pmod{4}$, which
is equivalent to $v_{2}(v-1)=1$, which in turn is equivalent to $v_{2}(\sigma)=1$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Let $f$ be an arbitrary arithmetic function. Then, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$
\[
 M_{f}(n):=\sum_{v=1}^{n} [v\perp n]f(\gcd(v-1,n)) = \varphi(n)\sum_{d\backslash n}\frac{(\mu * f)(d)}{\varphi(d)}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:local-counts}
Let $n=\prod_p p^{a}$ and write $e_{p}=v_p(\sigma)$ for the multiplicity of $p$ in the
prime factorization of $\sigma$.  Then
\[
 N_n(\sigma)=\prod_{p^{a}\backslash\backslash n}N_{p^a}(p^{e_{p}}),
\]
where
\[
 N_{p^a}(p^{e})=
 \begin{cases}
 p^{a-1}(p-2),&e=0,\\
 p^{a-e-1}(p-1),&1\le e<a,\\
 1,&e=a.
 \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Since the function $h(n)=\gcd(v-1,n)$ is multiplicative, the Chinese remainder theorem
allows us to study $N_{p^{a}}(p^{e})$ and then multiply the results. If we define $f(x)=[x=p^{e}]$ and
$e=v_{p}(\sigma)$ then $M_{f}(p^{a}) = N_{p^{a}}(p^{e})$ and
\begin{align*}
 N_{p^{a}}(p^{e}) &= \sum_{v=1}^{p^{a}}[v\perp p^{a}][\gcd(v-1,p^{a})=p^{e}]\\
 &=\varphi(p^{a})\sum_{d\backslash p^{a}}\frac{1}{\varphi(d)}\sum_{st=d}\mu(s)[t=p^{e}]\\
 &=\varphi(p^{a})\sum_{e\leq \ell\leq a}\frac{1}{\varphi(p^{\ell})}\mu(p^{\ell}/p^{e}).
\end{align*}

This simplifies to
\begin{align*}
N_{p^{a}}(p^{e}) &= \varphi(p^{a})\sum_{\ell=0}^{\min(1,a-e)}\frac{\mu(p^{\ell})}{\varphi(p^{e+\ell})}\\
&=\begin{cases}
\varphi(p^{a})\left(1-\frac{1}{\varphi(p)}\right), & e=0,\\
\varphi(p^{a})\left(\frac{1}{\varphi(p^{e})}-\frac{1}{\varphi(p^{e+1})}\right), & 1\leq e < a,\\
\varphi(p^{a})\cdot \frac{1}{\varphi(p^{a})}, & e=a,
\end{cases}\\
&=\begin{cases}
p^{a-1}(p-2), & e=0,\\
p^{a-e-1}(p-1), & 1\leq e < a,\\
1, & e=a.
\end{cases} \qedhere
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Note that $N_{n}(\sigma)$ and Proposition \ref{prop:local-counts} apply to every
positive integer $n$, including odd $n$, with $N_{1}(1)=1$. We will use this fact later.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
For even $n$
\[
S_{n}(\mathcal{T}_{n}) = C_{n}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The translations $e^{u}.1$ with $u\neq 0$ are precisely the translation derangements. Here $\sigma = n$ and $N=\frac{n}{n}=1$
in Lemma \ref{lem:compression}, so for $r\equiv -u \pmod{n}$ their product is
\[
\left(i\cot\frac{\pi r}{n}\right)^{n}.
\]

Since $n$ is even, $(-1)^{u}=(-1)^{r}$. Summing over $u=1,\ldots,n-1$ gives the result.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{Thm:DihDer} For even $n\geq 4$,
\[
S_{n}(\mathcal{D}_{n}) = C_{n}+[4\backslash n]\frac{n}{2}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The contribution of translations is $C_{n}$ by the preceding proposition. It remains to consider the reflections $e^{u}.-1:x\mapsto -x+u$. Such a reflection has a fixed point if and only if
\[
 2x \equiv u \pmod{n}
\]
has a solution. Since $n$ is even, it is a derangement only when $u$ is odd. Thus there are $n/2$ reflective derangements.  For a reflection $\sigma = \gcd(-2,n) = 2$ and $N=n/2$. If $n\equiv 2 \pmod{4}$, then $N$ is odd, $r\equiv -u \equiv 1\pmod{2}$, and Lemma \ref{lem:compression} gives
\[
\left(i\cot\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2} = 0.
\]

Thus all reflective derangements contribute zero. If $4\backslash n$, then $N$ is even and their product is $1$. For $u$ odd, Lemma \ref{lem:translation-sign} gives $\operatorname{sign}(e^{u}.1)=-1$. Taking the representative $v=n-1$ for $-1$ in Lemma \ref{lem:refl} we have
\[
 \operatorname{sign}(e^{0}.-1) = (-1)^{\frac{n-2}{2}} = -1,
\]
for $4\backslash n$. Hence every derangement reflection has positive sign, and their total contribution is $n/2$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
For even $n\geq 4$.
\[
S_{n}(\mathcal{Q}_{n}^{\mathrm{dih}}) = [4\backslash n]\frac{n}{2}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The only translation derangement that is involutive is the antipodal one: $e^{n/2}.1$. Its product vanishes because $\zeta^{-n/2}=-1$, so every factor has numerator $1+\zeta^{-n/2}=0$. Thus only reflective derangements contribute, and we know that their contribution is $\frac{n}{2}$ when $4\backslash n$, as was seen in the proof of Theorem \ref{Thm:DihDer}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
It is interesting to note that the sum for dihedral quasipolarities coincides with that for affine quasipolarities when $n/2$ is odd, and it retrieves a summand of the more general formula for $n/2$ even.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:reduction}
For even $n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:divisor-formula}
 S_n=\sum_{\substack{\sigma \backslash n\\\sigma\ \mathrm{even}}}
 \epsilon_n(\sigma)N_n(\sigma)\frac n\sigma\,J_{n,\sigma},
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Jnd}
 J_{n,\sigma}=
 \begin{cases}
 -1,&n/\sigma\text{ even},\\[5pt]
 \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\sigma-1}(-1)^r
 \left(i\cot\frac{\pi r}{\sigma}\right)^\sigma,&n/\sigma\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Group \eqref{eq:Sn} first by $\sigma=\gcd(1-v,n)$ and then by the nonzero
residue $r\equiv-u\pmod \sigma$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:compression} evaluates the
product.  Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-sign} shows that the translations in a fixed residue
class contribute $(n/\sigma)(-1)^r$.

The multiplication sign is constant among all $v$ satisfying
$\gcd(1-v,n)=\sigma$ and is equal to $\epsilon_n(\sigma)$, while the number of
such multipliers is $N_n(\sigma)$.  If $n/\sigma$ is even, then
$\Psi_{n,\sigma}(r)=1$ and, since $\sigma$ is even,
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^{\sigma-1}(-1)^r=-1.
\]
If $n/\sigma$ is odd, Lemma~\ref{lem:compression} gives the second line of
\eqref{eq:Jnd}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:2part}
If $n/\sigma$ is odd, then $\sigma$ contains the full $2$-primary part of $n$.
In particular $v_2(\sigma)=v_2(n)$, and hence
\[
 \epsilon_n(\sigma)=1
\]
throughout the cotangent case of \eqref{eq:Jnd}.  Thus the only
negative multiplication-sign correction occurs in the elementary
case $n/\sigma$ even.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
(Cvijovi\'{c}-Klinowski, 2000, \cite{CK00})
The polynomial
\[
p_{q}(x)=\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor\frac{q-1}{2}\rfloor}(-1)^{r}\binom{q}{2r+1}x^{q-2r-1}
\]
has simple roots
\[
x_{r} = \cot\frac{\pi r}{q}, \quad 1\leq r \leq q-1.
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:Cclosed}
For every even $\sigma$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Cclosed}
 C_\sigma=-2^\sigma\sum_{t=0}^{\sigma/2}
 r_{\sigma,t}\,
 \frac{B_{\sigma-2t}(1/2)}{(\sigma-2t)!}\,
 \sigma^{\sigma-2t},
\end{equation}
where $B_{j}(x)$ is the $j$-th Bernoulli polynomial, defined by
\[
 \frac{xe^{tx}}{e^{x}-1} = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}B_{j}(t)\frac{x^{j}}{j!}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Put $\sigma=2m$.  Liu and Xin prove
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^{\sigma-1}(-1)^r\cot^{2m}\frac{\pi r}{\sigma}
 =(-1)^{m+1}2^{2m}\sum_{t=0}^{m}
 r_{2m,t}\frac{B_{2(m-t)}(1/2)}{(2(m-t))!}
 \sigma^{2(m-t)}.
\]
Multiplication by $i^{2m}=(-1)^m$ yields \eqref{eq:Cclosed}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
For even $n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:final}
 S_n=-\sum_{\substack{\sigma\backslash n\\\sigma\ \mathrm{even}}}
 \epsilon_n(\sigma)N_n(\sigma)\frac n\sigma\left([2\backslash \tfrac{n}{\sigma}]+[2\centernot\backslash\tfrac{n}{\sigma}]2^\sigma\sum_{t=0}^{\sigma/2}
 r_{\sigma,t}\frac{B_{\sigma-2t}(1/2)}{(\sigma-2t)!}\sigma^{\sigma-2t}\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
If $\ell\geq 1$, then $S_{2^{\ell}}$ is an integer.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The values of $\sigma_{j} = [2\backslash j](-1)^{j/2}\frac{1}{q}\binom{q}{j+1}$ are integers. Indeed, suppose $q$ is a power
of $2$ and $\sigma_{j}\neq 0$. Then $j+1$ is odd and the recursion
\[
(j+1)\binom{q}{j+1}=q\binom{q-1}{j},
\]
together with the fact that $(j+1)\perp q$, gives us $q\backslash \binom{q}{j+1}$. By the Newton-Girard recursion, $C_{2^{\ell}}$ is a sum of integers, which was the only possible non-integral summand, for $\frac{2^{\ell}}{2^{\ell}}=1$ is odd.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
If $p>3$ is a prime, then $S_{2p}$ has denominator $p$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The only two even divisors of $2p$ are $2$ and $2p$. For $\sigma=2$ we have $n/2 = p$ is odd and $C_{2}=0$, while
for $\sigma = 2p$ we have $N_{2p}(\sigma)=1$, $\epsilon_{2p}(\sigma)=1$ and $n/\sigma = 1$, and thus $S_{n}=C_{2p}$.

Let $\zeta=\exp(\pi i/p)$, $\omega = \zeta^{2}$,
\[
 \alpha_{j}=\frac{1+\omega^{j}}{1-\omega^{j}} = i\cot\frac{\pi j}{p}
\]
for $1\leq j\leq p-1$ and
\[
\beta_{r}=\frac{1+\zeta^{r}}{1-\zeta^{r}}= i\cot\frac{\pi r}{2p}
\]
for $r$ odd.

We can write
\[
C_{2p} = A_{p}-B_{p}
\]
where
\[
 A_{p} = \sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\alpha_{j}^{2p}\quad\text{and}\quad B_{p} = \sum_{r=1}^{2p-1}[2\centernot\backslash r]\beta^{2p}_{r}.
\]

The $\alpha_{j}$ are the roots of the polynomial
\[
 F_{p}(x)=\frac{(x+1)^{p}-(x-1)^{p}}{2p}
\]
which expands as
\[
F_{p}(x) = x^{p-1}+\frac{1}{p}\binom{p}{3}x^{p-3}+\frac{1}{p}\binom{p}{5}x^{p-5}+\cdots+\frac{1}{p}.
\]

Note that all coefficients are integers except the last one since $\frac{1}{p}\binom{p}{j}$ is an integer, for the
numerators of $\binom{p}{j}$ are divisible by $p$ while their denominators are not.

On the other hand, for $r$ odd, $(\zeta^{r})^{p} = -1$ and $\zeta^{r}=\frac{\beta_{r}-1}{\beta_{r}+1}$, hence
$(\beta_{r}-1)^{p} = -(\beta_{r}+1)^{p}$, and thus the $p$ numbers $\beta_{r}$ are the roots of
\[
 G_{p}(x) = \frac{(x+1)^{p}+(x-1)^{p}}{2}.
\]

Newton-Girard formulas now ensure $B_{p}$ is an integer, so we can focus on $A_{p}$. If $e_{i}$ is
the $i$-th elementary symmetric function on $m$ variables and $p_{r}=\sum_{j}x_{j}^{r}$ are the power sums, then
\[
 E(t) = \prod_{j=1}^{m}(1+x_{j}t) = \sum_{r=0}^{m}e_{r}t^{r}
\]
(see \cite[pp. 19--23]{Macdonald}) and, in particular,
\begin{align*}
\log E(t) &= \sum_{j=1}^{m}\log(1+x_{j}t)\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{r-1}x_{j}^{r}\frac{t^{r}}{r}\\
&= \sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{r-1}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{j}^{r}\right)\frac{t^{r}}{r}\\
&= \sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{r-1}p_{r}\frac{t^{r}}{r}.
\end{align*}

From the expression for $F_{p}$ we have
\[
e_{j} = [2\backslash j]\frac{1}{p}\binom{p}{j+1},
\]
and, in particular,
\[
e_{2} = \frac{1}{p}\binom{p}{3}
\]
is an integer. We can write
\[
 E(t) = B(t) + \frac{t^{m}}{p} = B(t)\left(1+\frac{t^{m}}{pB(t)}\right),
\]
and note that $B(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t]$ and $B(0) = 1$. Taking logarithms we get
\[
\log E(t) = \log B(t) + \log\left(1+\frac{t^{m}}{pB(t)}\right),
\]
and note that for $F_{p}$ we have $m=p-1$ roots, and thus for $p\geq 5$ we have
\[
 3m = 3(p-1) > 2p = 2m+2.
\]

Since
\[
\log\left(1+\frac{t^{m}}{pB(t)}\right) = \frac{t^{m}}{pB(t)}-\frac{t^{2m}}{2p^{2} (B(t))^{2}} +\cdots
\]
then the terms $\frac{t^{jm}}{jp^{j}B(t)^{j}}$ for $j\geq 3$ do not contribute to the coefficient of $t^{2p}$, since $3m>2p$. Therefore
\[
\frac{A_{p}}{-2p}=[t^{2p}]\log E = [t^{2p}]\log B + \frac{1}{p}[t^{m+2}]B^{-1}-\frac{1}{2p^{2}}[t^{2}]B^{-2}.
\]

A term of the form
\[
 r[t^{r}]\log B =  [t^{r-1}]\frac{B'(t)}{B(t)}
\]
is an integer since the derivative of a polynomial with integer coefficients has integer coefficients and the
formal inverse of $B(t)$ has integer coefficients because $B(0) = 1$. In particular, $2p[t^{2p}]\log(B)$ is an integer. From
this we also deduce that
\[
2p\frac{1}{p}[t^{m+2}]B^{-1} = 2[t^{m+2}]B^{-1}
\]
is an integer. For the last term, we have
\begin{align*}
B(t) &= 1+e_{2}t^{2}+O(t^{4}),\\
B(t)^{-1} &= 1-e_{2}t^{2} + O(t^{4}),\\
B(t)^{-2} &= 1-2e_{2}t^{2}+O(t^{4}),
\end{align*}
which implies that
\[
-\frac{1}{2p^{2}}[t^{2}]B^{-2} = \frac{e_{2}}{p^{2}}.
\]
and thus
\[
A_{p} = -2p[t^{2p}]\log E(t) \equiv -\frac{2e_{2}}{p} \pmod{\mathbb{Z}}.
\]

Finally
\[
 e_{2} = \frac{1}{p}\binom{p}{3} = \frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{6} \equiv \frac{1}{3}\pmod{p},
\]
which means that $pA_{p} \equiv -2e_{2} \equiv -\frac{2}{3}\pmod{p}$. Since this is non-zero,
then the reduced denominator of $A_{p}$ is exactly $p$. Consequently the reduced denominator of $C_{2p}$
is exactly $p$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{L:Signo}
For $m\geq 2$
\[
\operatorname{sign}(C_{2m}) = (-1)^{m+1}
\]
and $C_{2}=0$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Since $i^{2m}=(-1)^{m}$, we can pair the terms $r$ and $2m-r$ in $C_{2m}$. The middle term $r=m$
vanishes because $\cot(\pi/2)=0$. Therefore
\[
 C_{2m} = 2(-1)^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}(-1)^{r}\left(\cot\frac{\pi r}{2m}\right)^{2m}
\]
and the terms
\[
a_{r} = \left(\cot\frac{\pi r}{2m}\right)^{2m}
\]
are strictly decreasing for $1\leq r \leq m-1$ because $\cot(x)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\pi/2)$. By
the properties of alternating sums, its sign is negative, and multiplying by $(-1)^{m}$ gives the result.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
For every even integer $n\geq 6$
\[
\operatorname{sign}(S_{n}) = (-1)^{n/2+1}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
When $n=2q$ with $q$ odd, every even divisor is of the form $\sigma = 2f$ with $f\backslash q$, which
means that $n/\sigma = q/f$ is odd. Hence only cotangent sums contribute to $S_{n}$. Furthermore,
$\epsilon_{n}(\sigma) = (-1)^{\frac{\sigma\cdot (n/2-1)}{2}}= 1$ since $n/2 = q$ is odd. By Lemma \ref{L:Signo}
\[
\operatorname{sign}(C_{2f})=(-1)^{f+1} = 1
\]
since $f>1$ is odd. For the $f=1$ term we have $C_{2}=0$, and thus all summands of $S_{n}$ are non-negative
when $n=2q\geq 6$. Since $N_{2q}(2q)=1$ and $C_{2q}>0$, it follows that $S_{2q}>0$.

When $n=2^{a}q$ with $a\geq 2$ and $q$ odd, the cotangent summands correspond to divisors of the form
$\sigma =2^{a}f$ with $f\backslash q$, because $n/\sigma$ must be odd. But then by Lemma \ref{L:Signo}
\[
 \operatorname{sign}(C_{\sigma}) = (-1)^{2^{a-1}f+1} = -1.
\]
and $\epsilon_{n}(\sigma) = 1$ because $\sigma/2$ is even.

The possible positive contributions then come from the cases $\sigma = 2^{e}f$ with $1\leq e < a$, $f\backslash q$.
Put
\[
 \mathcal{A}(q) = \sum_{f\backslash q} N_{q}(f)\frac{q}{f},
\]
which is positive. For the factors related to the prime $2$, note first that $n/\sigma$ is even, thus the contribution of $J_{n,\sigma}$ is a $-1$ factor. We first examine $e=1$, which contributes the positive term (since $\epsilon_{n}(\sigma)=-1$)
\[
N_{2^{a}}(2)\frac{2^{a}}{2^{1}}=2^{a-2}2^{a-1}=2^{2a-3};
\]
we follow with $2\leq e < a$, which contribute the negative terms (since $\epsilon_{n}(\sigma)=1$),
\[
N_{2^{a}}(2^{e})\frac{2^{a}}{2^{e}}=2^{a-e-1}2^{a-e} = 2^{2a-2e-1}.
\]

Thus the total contribution is
\begin{align*}
E_{n} &= \left(2^{2a-3}-\sum_{e=2}^{a-1}2^{2a-2e-1}\right)\mathcal{A}(q)\\
&=\left(2^{2a-3}-\sum_{e=0}^{a-3}2^{2a-2e-5}\right)\mathcal{A}(q)\\
&=\frac{2^{2a-2}+2}{2^{2}-1}\mathcal{A}(q)=\frac{2^{2a-2}+2}{3}\mathcal{A}(q)>0,
\end{align*}
and it is bounded above as follows: first $\sum_{f\backslash q} N_{q}(f)=\phi(q)$, and thus
\[
\mathcal{A}(q)\leq q \sum_{f\backslash q} N_{q}(f) = q \phi(q) \leq q^{2}.
\]

Since
\[
 \frac{2^{2a-2}+2}{3}\leq 2^{2a-2}
\]
for $a\geq 2$, then
\[
E_{n} \leq 2^{2a-2}q^{2} = \frac{(2^{a}q)^{2}}{2^{2}} = \frac{n^{2}}{4}.
\]

In order to bound $|C_{n}|$ from below for $n=2^{a}q\geq 8$, we first define
\[
a_{r} = \left(\cot\frac{r\pi}{n}\right)^{n}
\]
for $1\leq r\leq n/2-1$. Since $n/2$ is even, we can write
\[
|C_{n}|=2\sum_{r=1}^{n/2-1}(-1)^{r+1} a_{r} \geq 2(a_{1}-a_{2}).
\]

By the double angle formula for tangents, we have for $0<x<\pi/4$ that
\[
\frac{\cot 2x }{\cot x } = \frac{1-(\tan(x))^{2}}{2}< \frac{1}{2}
\]
and thus
\[
\frac{a_{2}}{a_{1}} = \frac{\left(\cot\frac{2\pi}{n}\right)^{n}}{\left(\cot\frac{\pi}{n}\right)^{n}}<\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n}.
\]

Since the cotangent is decreasing, then for $n\geq 8$
\[
\cot\frac{\pi}{n} \geq \cot \frac{\pi}{8} = 1+\sqrt{2} >2
\]
which means that $a_{1}=(\cot\frac{\pi}{n})^{n}>2^{n}$. Hence,
\[
 |C_{n}| \geq 2(a_{1}-a_{2}) \geq 2\left(a_{1}-\frac{a_{1}}{2^{n}}\right) > 2\cdot 2^{n}\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right)
 =2^{n+1}-2> \frac{n^{2}}{4}.
\]

Given that the absolute value of $C_{n}$ is larger than the upper bound on the largest positive contribution, and
other cotangent terms are also negative, it follows that $S_{n}<0$ for $n=2^{a}q$ with $a\geq 2$ and $q$ odd.
